The U.S. Supreme Court has given Apple a 24-hour reprieve, pausing a California court deadline that required the company to submit what commission rate (if any) it could collect on purchases made by users outside the App Store. Details below.

Apple Granted 24-Hour Reprieve

Yesterday, Judge Gonzalez Rogers denied Apple's request to pause the App Store fee proceedings, despite the Supreme Court reviewing the company's appeal of a contempt ruling.

Background: When Judge Gonzalez Rogers issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, Apple responded by allowing external links but charging a 27% commission on purchases made through those links.

Judge Gonzalez Rogers subsequently found Apple in violation of the injunction, ruling it in contempt of court. The Supreme Court ultimately agreed to review that ruling, with Apple arguing the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit it from collecting commissions.

Although the Supreme Court is reviewing the contempt ruling, the case continues in the lower court, where Judge Gonzalez Rogers will determine how much commission (if any) Apple can collect on purchases made outside the App Store.

Apple had asked Judge Gonzalez Rogers to pause these proceedings while the Supreme Court considered the contempt case, but the judge denied Apple's request yesterday and gave the company until 5 p.m. today to submit its proposed fees and supporting evidence.

However, Apple filed an emergency application with the Supreme Court (as reported by Bloomberg), and Justice Kagan temporarily granted it, pausing the lower court proceedings until 5 p.m. Thursday, while the Supreme Court considers Apple's request for a longer-term stay.

Bloomberg reports:

This means the Supreme Court has the opportunity to grant Apple's longer-term stay request, setting aside the lower court's fee proceedings while it reviews the contempt ruling.
